title: The valley that farms rice and fish in the same field
standfirst: Arunachal Pradesh keeps its best valley behind a permit, which is most of why you have not heard of it.
body: Ziro sits in the Lower Subansiri district of Arunachal Pradesh, a flat green bowl of paddy fields ringed by pine ridges. It is home to the Apatani, who grow rice and fish in the same flooded field — a system that uses no draught animals and no machinery, and which has kept the valley on UNESCO's tentative list for years.

The valley is small enough to cycle across in a morning and quiet enough that most travellers overshoot it entirely on the way to Tawang. That is the argument for going: not that it is spectacular the way the high Himalaya is spectacular, but that it is a working landscape people still live inside.

Late September brings the Ziro Festival of Music, running 24–27 September in 2026. Started in 2012 by Bobby Hano and Anup Kutty, it is hosted by the Apatani, builds its stages from local bamboo, and runs a zero-plastic policy. It is also when the valley is least like itself — worth going for, or worth avoiding, depending entirely on what you came for.

title: Three hours from Tbilisi to the wall of the Caucasus
standfirst: Georgia's most photographed church sits on a ridge most people reach before lunch. The paperwork changed this year.
body: Stepantsminda — still widely called Kazbegi — is a small town at the top of the Georgian Military Highway, close enough to Tbilisi that people day-trip it and far enough into the Caucasus that they regret doing so.

Above the town, Gergeti Trinity Church stands alone on a ridge with Mount Kazbek rising behind it. You can drive most of the way up. Walking it takes a couple of hours and changes the experience entirely.

Two things Indian travellers should know before booking. Georgia is an e-visa country: apply at evisa.gov.ge, around USD 20, roughly 5–7 working days, and there is now a mandatory DuVerify identity step after payment. Separately, since 1 January 2026 every tourist must carry health and accident insurance covering at least 30,000 GEL. Neither is difficult. Both catch people out at the airport.

title: The Malaysia window closes on 31 December
standfirst: Indians still enter Malaysia visa-free for 30 days — but the exemption is dated, and there is a form most people miss.
body: Malaysia has waived entry visas for Indian nationals since December 2023, and the Home Ministry has extended that waiver to 31 December 2026. It covers tourism, business, social visits and transit for up to 30 days. It does not cover work or study, cannot be extended, and cannot be converted to another visa type once you are in the country.

The part that catches people is the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card. It is mandatory, it is free, and it must be submitted online before you travel — guidance says at least three days ahead. Turning up without it is not a formality you sort out at the counter.
You will also need a passport valid six months beyond entry, a confirmed onward or return ticket inside the 30 days, and an address you can show. None of it is difficult. All of it is checked.
Worth knowing rather than assuming: this is an extension with an end date on it, not a permanent change. If you are planning a Malaysia trip for 2027, check again before you book.

title: Ladakh or Spiti
standfirst: Two high-altitude deserts, one long argument. People who have done both rarely rank them the way first-timers expect.
question: You have ten days and one shot at the Himalaya. Which one?

optionA.name: Ladakh
optionA.pitch: Bigger, higher, easier to reach. You can fly into Leh and be on a high pass the next day.
optionA.against: That accessibility is the problem. The main circuit is busy, and altitude sickness hits people who skipped acclimatisation because the flight made it feel easy.

optionB.name: Spiti
optionB.pitch: Harder to get to, and quieter for exactly that reason. The road in does the acclimatising for you.
optionB.against: No airport. The Manali–Kaza route over Kunzum La typically opens late May to mid-June and closes by late October, and the Gramphu–Losar stretch is broken road with water crossings.

body: The honest split: Ladakh is the better first trip and Spiti is the better second one. Ladakh gives you scale immediately. Spiti gives you the version of the same landscape where you can hear it.

One practical note that decides it for a lot of people — Spiti's window is narrower than Ladakh's, and the pass status changes with snowfall. Check Border Roads Organisation advisories close to your dates rather than trusting a blog from last season.

title: The Gulf city that never traded its old town for towers
standfirst: Four hours from most Indian metros, and the least Dubai-like place on the Arabian peninsula.
body: Muscat is low. There is a building height limit and a rule about white walls, so the city runs along the coast in a thin line of flat-roofed houses between black volcanic hills and the sea rather than piling upward. After the Gulf's glass cities, the effect is disorienting in a good way.

The Muttrah corniche is where you start. A working harbour on one side, the old souq on the other, Portuguese-era watchtowers on the ridges above, and a walk you can do at sunset in half an hour. The souq sells frankincense because Oman actually produces it, not because tourists expect it.

The practical case for Oman over its neighbours: it is close, it is cheap by Gulf standards, and it has mountains and wadis within a couple of hours of the capital. The practical case against: summer is genuinely punishing, and almost everything worth doing is outdoors.

title: Bridges that are grown, not built, and take decades
standfirst: Khasi communities train fig roots across rivers over a generation. India has just put them forward for UNESCO.
body: In the Khasi and Jaintia Hills, people cross rivers on bridges made from the living roots of rubber fig trees, trained across the water over years until they can carry a person. They are called jingkieng jri. They connect more than 75 remote villages in one of the wettest inhabited places on earth, and unlike concrete they get stronger with age.

In January 2026 India submitted the nomination dossier to UNESCO — the Jingkieng Jri cultural landscape, for the 2026-27 cycle. That is a submission, not an inscription, and the process takes time. But it is the clearest signal yet that these stop being a local curiosity and start being a queue.

Go for the villages rather than the single famous double-decker bridge. The walk down is long, the walk back up is longer, and the wettest months are exactly when the region is at its most extraordinary and its most difficult.

title: The cheapest good idea for an Indian passport right now
standfirst: Sri Lanka's hill country is a short flight, a free entry permit, and a train ride people plan whole trips around.
body: Ella is a small town in Sri Lanka's hill country, surrounded by tea estates and reached by a train line that people book trips around rather than merely tolerate. The Kandy to Ella stretch runs slowly through tea country with the doors open, which is most of the point.

What makes it unusually easy for Indian travellers in 2026 is the paperwork, or the lack of it. The tourist ETA is free for Indian passport holders — 30 days, double entry — and the flight from South India is short enough to make a five-day trip make sense.
Apply for the ETA online at eta.gov.lk before you fly even though it is free and even though arrival counters exist. Third-party sites charge for something the government does not.

title: Sri Lanka stopped charging Indians to enter
standfirst: The tourist ETA is now free for 40 nationalities, India among them. The catch is who you apply through.
body: Sri Lanka's free tourist ETA scheme took effect on 25 May 2026 following parliamentary approval earlier that month, extending fee-free entry to nationals of 40 countries. India is on the list, alongside the UK, the US, the UAE and Saudi Arabia.
For an Indian passport that means 30 days, double entry, and nothing to pay. It applies to tourism, and the fee waiver was confirmed across tourist, business and transit categories.

The thing worth knowing is not the rule but the scams around it. Because the ETA is free, the value has moved to intermediaries who charge a 'service fee' for filling in a government form. Apply at eta.gov.lk. Anything asking for money is not the government.
You can still be processed on arrival at Colombo, but doing it online first is the difference between walking through and queueing.

title: Thailand's paper form is gone. The new one is easy to miss.
standfirst: Every non-Thai arrival now needs a digital arrival card, submitted before you fly. It is free, and there is a 72-hour window.
body: The old TM6 card — the one handed out on the plane and filled in with a borrowed pen — was retired on 1 May 2025. In its place is the Thailand Digital Arrival Card, submitted online before you arrive, and required of every non-Thai national entering by air, land or sea.

Two details catch people. It can only be submitted within 72 hours of arrival, so doing it a fortnight early when you remember does not work. And it is single-entry: hop to Laos for a weekend and come back, and you need a fresh one.
It is free on the government portal. Sites charging a 'processing fee' for it are charging you for a form you can fill in yourself in five minutes.

Small upside if you are organised: since March 2026 many travellers can use automated border gates, where facial recognition matches you against the arrival card and passport already on file. The queue you skip is the reward for doing the paperwork.

title: A city with mountains at the end of the street, and no visa required
standfirst: Indians have walked into Kazakhstan without a visa since 2022. Almost nobody has noticed.
body: Almaty sits hard against the Tian Shan, close enough that you can be on a chairlift in the mountains within an hour of leaving the city centre. It is green, Soviet-planned, full of tree-lined avenues, and priced like nowhere else at that latitude.
The reason to know about it now is procedural. Indian passport holders have had visa-free access since February 2022 — no application, no fee, no e-visa portal. You turn up with a passport.

The limit is the part to read carefully. Fourteen days per visit, and no more than forty-two days total in any rolling 180-day period. Fine for a week of mountains. Not a place to base yourself for a season.
One more thing that trips people: if you are staying with a friend rather than a hotel, your host has to register you within three business days. Hotels handle it for you. A spare room does not.

title: Thailand or Vietnam
standfirst: The first Southeast Asia trip almost always comes down to these two. They are not the same holiday.
question: Ten days, first time in Southeast Asia, flying from India. Which?

optionA.name: Thailand
optionA.pitch: Easier in every practical sense. More direct flights from more Indian cities, infrastructure built for first-timers, and you can be on a beach the same day you land.
optionA.against: That ease is the trade. The well-known routes are busy, and it is possible to spend ten days in Thailand without meeting a Thai person who is not being paid to talk to you.

optionB.name: Vietnam
optionB.pitch: Longer and narrower, so a trip becomes a route rather than a base — north to south, or the reverse. Food is the best argument, and it is cheaper day to day.
optionB.against: More moving. Domestic flights or overnight trains eat time you might have spent still. And it needs an e-visa applied for online before you fly, where Thailand does not.

body: The paperwork is not the deciding factor but it is worth knowing: Thailand needs no visa in advance for many travellers, only the digital arrival card within 72 hours of landing. Vietnam requires an e-visa applied for at the government portal, evisa.gov.vn, before you travel.
The honest split: Thailand is the better first trip and Vietnam is the better second one. Thailand teaches you the region. Vietnam rewards you for already knowing how to move through it.

title: The town that survived by being too poor to knock down
standfirst: Hoi An kept its old trading quarter because the river silted up and the money left. Now that is the whole reason to go.
body: Hoi An was a working port for centuries, trading with Japanese and Chinese merchants who left their architecture behind. When the river silted and shipping moved to Da Nang, the town stopped growing — and the old quarter was never demolished to make room for anything newer.
It is small enough to walk end to end, and the strongest hours are early morning before the tour buses and late evening once they have gone.
Da Nang is thirty minutes away and does the opposite job: a real working city with a long beach, useful as a base if Hoi An by itself feels too curated.

title: The country that charges you by the night to be there
standfirst: Bhutan meters tourism deliberately. Indians pay a fraction of what everyone else does — and do not need a tour operator.
body: Bhutan is the rare country that has decided it does not want more visitors than it can absorb, and prices accordingly. Every tourist pays a Sustainable Development Fee per person per night, which funds healthcare, education and conservation.

Indian nationals are treated differently in two ways that matter. They do not need a visa — a permit instead — and they pay a regional rate far below the international one. They are also not required to book through a licensed tour operator, which most other nationalities are.
The practical effect is that Bhutan is within reach of an Indian traveller in a way it simply is not for most people, and you can structure the trip yourself rather than buying a package.
